text: A company running workloads in both Azure and AWS eventually needs one question answered without opening two separate consoles: how much compute is actually running in each cloud right now, and how do the two compare? This lesson builds that reconciliation report, combining everything from this chapter into one script.

az vm list with JSON output returns every VM as an array. Piped into jq with the identity filter and length, it counts that array's elements in one step and stores the result in a variable — no for loop required just to get a total, the way earlier lessons needed one to check each item individually.

The AWS side reuses Lesson 15's select() pattern on describe-instances, but wraps the filtered result in square brackets to build a new array containing only non-terminated instances, then takes length of that array. Terminated instances can still show up in the response for a while, so excluding them keeps the count honest.

Comparing the two totals needs two new small pieces. Dollar-double-parentheses is bash arithmetic expansion — it adds the two counts as numbers, unlike dollar-parentheses which runs a command. -gt is a numeric greater-than test inside square brackets, the direct counterpart to the == string test from Lesson 14, feeding an if/elif/else that reacts to whichever cloud has more.

The complete script, multi-cloud-inventory.sh, counts Azure VMs, counts non-terminated AWS instances, adds them into a combined total, and prints which cloud has more or calls it even. Every piece of it — az and aws with JSON output, jq doing the counting, and the shebang-variable-if pattern — came directly from this chapter and the shell-scripting basics before it.

That's a real multi-cloud inventory report, built from nothing but bash, two CLIs, and jq. But counting what already exists is only half the job — the next chapter turns to Infrastructure as Code, starting with what a single ground-truth definition solves that a script run by hand never fully can.
